figures.title: What training actually does
figures.caption: The 1,037 state variables choose regimes; the forecast equation has only five coefficients. The forest averages separately grown trees. It does not optimize one neural-network loss over epochs.

figures.title: What the losses mean
figures.caption: Top is the actual forecast scoring rule, not a fitted curve. Bottom summarizes the local leaf objective in standardized units. The source's split criterion differs from its terminal-fit objective; there is no single globally minimized training loss.

figures.title: Training versus forecasting calendar
figures.caption: Representations stop at the last training origin, one quarter before the training target cutoff. Forecasting is h=1 with observed lag updates, not an eight-step recursive path. The model is refitted every two years.

figures.title: The large state and the small equation
figures.caption: The state is large relative to the training history. Trees select splits rather than fitting 1,037 regression slopes. This is a capacity/noise concern, not proof that overfitting caused the forecast gap.

figures.title: Recorded preprocessing diagnostics
figures.caption: These are recorded counts, not per-iteration loss histories. All six state rebuilds agreed exactly with the frozen inputs. The original run did not retain a factor-completion objective trajectory.

figures.title: The actual result versus the paper
figures.caption: All 48 quarters and all seeds. Fixed FA-AR is 0.833; MRF is 0.824–0.852, not 0.72. *Same-equation OLS is a new post-hoc control with the MRF's four slope terms, not the paper's nine-coefficient FA-AR or a replacement primary.

figures.title: A useful nuance: better MAE, little or no RMSE gain
figures.caption: All three MRF seeds have lower MAE than fixed FA-AR and the exploratory static control. They do not uniformly improve the primary RMSE metric. Squaring errors makes rare large misses more costly. The dashed line is each metric's fixed FA-AR value; reporting MAE does not change the primary criterion.

figures.title: Actual versus forecast changes
figures.caption: The target is the quarterly change in log unemployment, multiplied by 100 for readability. These are log points, not unemployment-rate percentage-point changes.

figures.title: Where the large miss happens
figures.caption: In 2009Q1 the actual log change is 0.1856, fixed FA-AR predicts 0.1185, and MRF predicts 0.0881/0.1034/0.0969. The forest underreacts more than the fixed-factor comparator at this quarter.

figures.title: Forecasts in familiar units
figures.caption: Each level forecast equals the observed previous-quarter unemployment rate × exp(predicted log change). It is a sequence of one-step forecasts with observed lag updates, not a recursive multi-year forecast. Main scoring stays in the original log-change target.

figures.title: Rolling forecast error
figures.caption: Overlapping trailing eight-quarter windows are descriptive and dependent. They were not used to choose settings, seeds or a favorable evaluation interval.

figures.title: When the forest helps or hurts
figures.caption: Post-hoc calendar windows, not official recession dates. MRF improves 8–11% before 2008, but has 4–11% higher RMSE in 2008–09 and 3–4% higher RMSE in 2010–14. This is diagnosis, not a newly chosen benchmark.

figures.title: Prediction range and underreaction
figures.caption: Dashed line is perfect prediction. Slopes regress forecasts on actuals for description only; they are not probability calibration tests or fitted forecast corrections. Only 48 points per panel.

figures.title: Residuals through time
figures.caption: A residual here is forecast minus actual, so negative errors mean the rise in unemployment was underpredicted. All residual plots use held-out target dates.

figures.title: Where the squared loss comes from
figures.caption: Identical color scale for every method. No normalization within rows; this preserves the magnitude of unusually costly quarters.

figures.title: How small wins and large losses accumulate
figures.caption: This accumulates each seed's squared error minus fixed FA-AR squared error. It is not a sequential model-selection rule. The 2009Q1 jump offsets many earlier gains.

figures.title: The six most expensive relative misses per seed
figures.caption: Quarters are ranked after observing results, solely to locate failures. These are individual contributions to total excess squared loss, not independently selected test tasks.

figures.title: Do errors depend on the forecast size?
figures.caption: Residual-versus-fitted diagnostic, using held-out forecasts. Patterns may reflect rare regimes or misspecification; this small sample cannot identify a unique cause.

figures.title: Tails and unusual errors
figures.caption: Only 48 held-out quarters. Q–Q lines describe the empirical error distribution, not an assumed Gaussian predictive distribution or a calibrated interval.

figures.title: Is forecast error serially structured?
figures.caption: Descriptive autocorrelations, with denominator equal to the full centered error sum of squares. No iid significance bands or multiple-testing claims are added to this 48-quarter sample.

figures.title: All five changing coefficients
figures.caption: Units are the saved original-scale coefficients; the intercept is in Δlog units. Vertical lines mark refits. PCA factors are refitted and can change sign/rotation: F1/F2 coefficients across boundaries are not an invariant economic quantity or a causal effect.

figures.title: What actually contributes to each forecast
figures.caption: These terms sum to every saved forecast within numerical precision. Contributions are predictive accounting, not causal attribution. The individual F1/F2 decomposition is tied to each refit's PCA basis.

figures.title: What the nonlinear model changes versus its own static equation
figures.caption: Post-hoc same-equation OLS isolates the addition of dynamic fitting more closely than the larger paper FA-AR equation. MRF has 0.6–4.1% higher RMSE than this control. No model was refitted using test outcomes, and this control does not replace the preregistered benchmark.

figures.title: Which indicators enter the two equation factors?
figures.caption: Twelve largest absolute loadings in the first refit (through 2002Q3 origin data). Signs are conventional, and PCA factors are statistical summaries, not identified structural causes or validated economic labels.

figures.title: Seed sensitivity versus the common forecasting error
figures.caption: The three seeds' forecasts correlate above 0.997 with one another. Narrow seed spread is not calibrated uncertainty: all seeds can make the same large mistake.

figures.title: Performance by refit block
figures.caption: Only eight targets per block, so these ratios are noisy. They locate instability; they do not prove a regime mechanism or authorize choosing a different model in each block.

figures.title: Training loss versus number of trees
figures.caption: New storage-only replay: first refit, seed 101, all 100 trees. Final forecasts and all coefficients match the original saved fit. The training curve is in-sample and optimistic; the orange curve is the already-observed next eight test quarters. Neither curve is a new validation set or a rule for selecting the tree count. Test and training periods have different difficulty.

figures.title: How averaging more trees changes each forecast
figures.caption: The eight forecasts from the same first-window replay. Trees are added in their original random order, not trained to correct previous trees' residuals. The fixed 100-tree choice is unchanged.

figures.title: The distribution of individual tree forecasts
figures.caption: These are 100 correlated model components from one fit, not 100 independent future outcomes. Tree dispersion is not a posterior, prediction interval or calibrated confidence band.

figures.title: How complex are the fitted trees?
figures.caption: Retained trees from the first-window replay only. NOBS counts rows used in the split sample, not every training outcome used by the final leaf regression or its neighboring-row smoother.

figures.title: What the trees actually split on
figures.caption: Usage frequency, not permutation importance or causal attribution. More numerous groups have more opportunities; correlated features can substitute for each other. Ancestor splits shared by leaves are counted once per tree node.
